guides.title: Check and fix your Open Graph image
guides.description: Find missing, blocked or incorrect Open Graph images. Check the URL, downloaded dimensions, alternative text and declared image metadata.
guides.answer: og:image identifies the image that represents a page when a service reads its Open Graph metadata. The tag points to an image URL, not a page containing the image. A successful page request does not prove that the image can be downloaded.
guides.intent: Inspect a missing, blocked or incorrectly sized share image.
checks: Inspect the final page URL. Read the first og:image value in the HTML head and open its absolute HTTP or HTTPS URL.
Check the image response independently. Confirm it returns image bytes rather than a sign-in page, redirect loop or error document.
Compare the downloaded width and height with og:image:width and og:image:height. Use the asset’s real dimensions; changing the tags does not resize the file.
Add og:image:alt that describes the actual image. The Open Graph protocol recommends alternative text when og:image is present.
guides.example:
<meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/share.png">
<meta property="og:image:width" content="1200">
<meta property="og:image:height" content="630">
<meta property="og:image:alt" content="The dashboard showing a completed preview check">
guides.limitation: The example dimensions describe one asset. Open Graph does not require a universal image size. Each consuming service can crop, cache or reject images differently. Metaprev’s web inspector accepts PNG, JPEG, WebP and GIF up to 5 MB; the local CLI supports additional inspection paths.

source.name: Open Graph protocol: image structured properties

guides.title: Check your Open Graph title and its fallback
guides.description: See which share title is present, distinguish og:title from the HTML title and X overrides, and fix missing or stale share headlines.
guides.answer: og:title supplies the title of a page as it should appear in a social graph. It is one of the four basic properties required by the Open Graph protocol. An HTML title or an X-specific title is a different field, even when a preview tool uses it as a fallback.
guides.intent: Resolve a missing or unexpected share headline.
checks: Inspect the deployed URL rather than the source file. Confirm og:title exists in the initial HTML head.
Compare og:title with the page title. Make each truthful for its context; the social title does not have to include every navigation or search suffix.
Check twitter:title separately if X needs different copy. Metaprev shows the field it observed rather than inventing a headline.
After a deployment, inspect again. If Metaprev sees the new title but a service still shows the old one, investigate that service’s cache with its own tools.
guides.example:
<title>Preview inspector · Example</title>
<meta property="og:title" content="See your link before you share it">
<meta name="twitter:title" content="A preview check before you post">
guides.limitation: Metaprev renders representative cards. It cannot clear a platform cache, guarantee that a consumer uses a fallback, or prove that all readers see the same headline. There is no universal Open Graph title character limit in the protocol.

guides.title: Check your Open Graph description
guides.description: Inspect a missing or stale share description, compare it with the page description, and add factual supporting copy to your metadata.
guides.answer: og:description gives a short description of the object represented by a page. The Open Graph protocol lists it as optional metadata. A consuming service may have its own requirements or choose not to display it, so a missing description and a hidden description are different problems.
guides.intent: Find why the supporting copy is missing or unexpected.
checks: Read og:description from the fetched HTML head. Do not assume that a visible paragraph on the page becomes the share description.
Compare og:description with meta name="description". Metaprev can use the page description as a representative fallback, while keeping the observed fields separate.
Write a factual description that explains the page. Avoid adding unsupported promises or padding the text to an arbitrary target length.
Inspect twitter:description if X copy differs. Recheck after deployment, then distinguish an outdated platform cache from outdated HTML.
guides.example:
<meta name="description" content="Inspect the tags and image behind a public link.">
<meta property="og:description" content="Check your share title, image and metadata before posting.">
guides.limitation: A tag can be present while a card omits the supporting text. Card layout, available space, platform policy and caching remain outside this inspection. The Open Graph protocol does not define one universal description length.

guides.title: Check the canonical URL in your Open Graph tags
guides.description: Compare the inspected URL, redirects, og:url and the HTML canonical. Find staging addresses or wrong page identities before sharing.
guides.answer: og:url identifies the canonical URL of the object represented by a page. The Open Graph protocol treats this URL as the object’s permanent identifier. It is distinct from the address originally entered into a preview tool and from the final address after HTTP redirects.
guides.intent: Find incorrect share identities and staging URLs.
checks: Inspect the public URL you intend to share. Note the final URL after redirects and compare it with og:url.
Check that og:url identifies the intended page. A copied homepage URL on every article can give different pages the same declared social identity.
Compare the HTML rel="canonical" link as a separate field. Investigate accidental staging domains, insecure schemes or unrelated paths.
When query parameters are part of the actual page identity, preserve the intended canonical policy. Do not strip all parameters just because they exist.
guides.limitation: Metaprev reports observed metadata and redirects. It does not choose your canonical policy, change a search engine’s selected canonical, or prove that social services merge identities in the same way.

guides.title: Choose the first image in your Open Graph tags
guides.description: Find conflicting image tags and choose a deliberate first image for a shared page.
guides.answer: Multiple og:image tags describe multiple images. The Open Graph protocol gives the first tag preference when values conflict. Each image’s structured properties belong immediately after its root tag.
checks: Read the deployed head in document order. Record every og:image tag.
Find which layout, page or plugin adds each tag. Remove accidental duplicates at their source.
Put the intended primary image first and keep its width, height and alt text together. Inspect the deployed result again.
guides.example:
<meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/primary.png">
<meta property="og:image:alt" content="Primary product view">
<meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/detail.png">
<meta property="og:image:alt" content="Product detail">
guides.limitation: Tag order is a declared preference. It does not guarantee a consumer’s final image selection.

guides.title: Choose an Open Graph type for a page
guides.description: Distinguish a general website page from an article when setting og:type.
guides.answer: og:type declares the kind of object a page represents. Choose a type that describes the page, then check that type’s additional properties.
guides.intent: Correct a copied or inappropriate object type.
checks: Check the fetched og:type. Do not infer it from the visual layout.
Use website for a general site page, or article for an actual article. Check the protocol before choosing a more specific type.
Keep title, URL and image consistent with the same object; inspect the page after deployment.
guides.example:
<meta property="og:type" content="website">
<meta property="og:title" content="Example preview tool">
<meta property="og:url" content="https://example.com/">
<meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/share.png">
guides.limitation: Changing the type does not force a platform to use a particular card layout.

guides.title: Check Open Graph metadata in Next.js
guides.description: Trace Next.js share metadata from its server component to the deployed page and image.
guides.answer: Next.js supports a metadata object, generateMetadata, and file conventions for Open Graph images. Metadata exports belong in Server Components. Start by identifying which mechanism owns the affected route.
guides.intent: Find the source of missing Next.js share metadata.
checks: Check the page and parent layouts for metadata exports. Inspect file-based opengraph-image assets too.
For a fixed page, define a metadata object in its server page or layout. Use the actual public origin and image.
Deploy, then inspect the final URL and image independently. Compare the fetched values with the intended route.
guides.limitation: This is an App Router example. Dynamic metadata can stream, and crawler handling can differ. A head-only inspection does not prove what every bot receives.

guides.title: Fix a share image URL that returns HTML
guides.description: Check whether the image address returns real image bytes or an error, login or document response.
guides.answer: A file extension is not proof of an image response. The Content-Type header describes the response media type. Check the response body as well as its headers.
guides.intent: Diagnose an image address that returns the wrong content.
checks: Request the exact image URL from the fetched og:image tag. Follow redirects and note the final status.
Check Content-Type and the downloaded file. A login page with a .png URL is still HTML.
Correct the public asset route or storage permissions, then inspect again without relying on your signed-in browser.
guides.limitation: Use this command only for a trusted public URL. Correct headers alone do not establish valid image bytes or platform acceptance.

guides.title: Trace redirects before checking a share preview
guides.description: Find whether a shared address reaches the intended page or redirects to a login, old route or wrong domain.
guides.answer: An HTTP redirect sends the client to another address using a redirect status and Location header. Diagnose the final destination before editing metadata on the original route.
guides.intent: Find the page a shared URL actually reaches.
checks: Request the shared address and record each Location value. Check HTTP-to-HTTPS and domain redirects.
Confirm the final response is the intended public page. Resolve loops or sign-in redirects before changing its tags.
Inspect the final page and compare its og:url with the intended shared identity.
guides.limitation: A browser may follow script-based navigation that a metadata fetcher does not execute. Metaprev bounds redirects; it does not emulate a browser session.

guides.title: Diagnose an old share image after deployment
guides.description: Separate stale page HTML, cached image bytes and a platform’s saved preview.
guides.answer: A page and its image are separate resources and can have different cache lifetimes. A fresh page response can still point to an older cached image. Check both layers before changing the metadata again.
guides.intent: Locate the layer serving an outdated image.
checks: Inspect the deployed page and confirm the current image URL. If the tag is old, investigate the page deployment or cache first.
Download that image and compare its bytes with the new asset. Review Cache-Control and validation headers at the origin and CDN.
When appropriate for your asset pipeline, publish the changed image at a versioned URL and update the tag. Recheck before investigating a platform-specific cache.
guides.limitation: A new asset URL does not clear every social platform’s page cache. Metaprev cannot invalidate third-party caches.
